title: A Simple Way To Curb Side-Talking
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers a four-step, student-empowered strategy for reducing disruptive side-talking without requiring teacher involvement in every incident. Teachers first clearly define what side-talking is (and when, if ever, it's acceptable), then equip students with a simple, polite hand gesture—like crossed fingers with a light shake—to signal a classmate to stop talking. The gesture is modeled and practiced as an inherently polite reminder rather than an aggressive rebuke, along with the appropriate receiving response of a quick nod. Because responsibility shifts to peers policing themselves, teachers can enforce consequences with certainty when the gesture itself is ignored, eliminating the common problem of not knowing who initiated the disruption.
points: Step 1: Clearly define side-talking for students, including any contexts where limited talking is allowed.
Step 2: Provide students a simple, non-offensive hand gesture (e.g., crossed fingers, lightly shaken) to signal 'I can't talk right now.'
Step 3: Model and role-play the gesture explicitly, including practicing at a student's desk during simulated instruction.
Step 4: Emphasize the gesture is a polite reminder, not an aggressive rebuke, and pair it with a quick nod as the appropriate response.
Because the strategy shifts responsibility to peers, teachers can enforce consequences with certainty when the routine itself is ignored—no more guessing who started the side-talking.
quotes: Side-talking can be especially frustrating because, although it’s done out of earshot, it’s remarkably disruptive.
Furthermore, side-talking begets more side-talking, as students catch the contagion and pass it along to others.
What follows is a simple, four-step solution. And the best part is, because it’s a student-empowered strategy, you don’t even have to get involved.
Crossing the first two fingers and shaking lightly is a good way to go. It’s a gesture conspicuous enough for you to see from across the room and all students can perform it easily.
It’s important to emphasize that the gesture is nothing more than a polite reminder to a friend. It’s like saying, “I’m sorry, but I can’t talk right now.
But unlike struggling to figure out who is deserving of a consequence, and getting it wrong much of the time, you’ll be able to tell exactly who the culprit is.
